Topic-Initiator: A Proactive Chatbot with Personalized Topic RAG
for Enhancing Willingness to Converse
Kazuya Matsuo Atsushi Otsuka, Narichika Nomoto, Makoto Nakatsuji
Human Informatics Labs., NTT, Inc.
kazuya.matsuo@ntt.com
Abstract
Stimulating users’ conversational willingness to converse remains a major challenge in chatbot research. Most ex-
isting chatbots respond passively to user inputs, relying on users to select conversation topics, which often reduces
their willingness. To address this issue, we propose, Topic-Initiator, a proactive chatbot that initiates conversations
with new topics aligned to user interests. It gathers information from external sources (e.g., the web) to obtain
potentially novel and engaging topics. To support this capability, we also introduce a novel Retrieval-Augmented
Generation (RAG) framework, Personalized-Topic RAG (PT-RAG), designed to retrieve new and interesting topics
for each user. Unlike existing RAG methods that fails to surface unseen information, PT-RAG leverages the infer-
ence capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify content that matches the user’s interests but is not
yet known to them. Speciﬁcally, PT-RAG estimates a user’s interests and knowledge from past interactions and or-
ganizes collected information into categories. Then, it uses an LLM to select a category that matches their interests
and obtain information not seen in their knowledge from the selected category. Automatic and human evaluations
demonstrate that PT-RAG retrieves new and interesting information more accurately and that Topic-Initiator signiﬁ-
cantly enhances users’ willingness to converse compared to existing methods.
Keywords: chatbot, dialogue system, RAG

2.
Related Work
2.1.
Proactive Chatbots
Extensive research has been conducted on proac-
tive chatbots and dialogue systems (Deng et al.,
2023a).
Tang et al. (2019); Wu et al. (2019);
Wang et al. (2023a,b); Deng et al. (2023b) pro-
posed dialogue systems that set conversational
goals and actively guide users toward achieving
them.
Xie et al. (2021) introduced a method in
which dialogue systems proactively generate ut-
terances to switch topics during casual conversa-
tions. Although these studies aim to build proac-
tive chatbots similar to ours, they overlook sce-
narios in which the chatbot itself initiates the con-
versation―a key distinction in our work. Li et al.
(2023) proposed a method where chatbots en-
gage in conversations by exploring trending news.
While this approach enables a chatbot to proac-
tively initiate conversations, it differs from our work
in that it disregards user interests and relies on
ﬁxed topics.
2.2.
Personalized Chatbots
Numerous studies have also explored personal-
ized chatbots and dialogue systems (Chen et al.,
2024).
The term ”personalized” has two def-
initions (Chen et al., 2024):
(1) generating re-
sponses consistent with the system’s own per-
sona, and (2) generating responses tailored to the
user’s persona. Our work focuses on the latter.
Zhong et al. (2022) proposed a method that
generates responses using proﬁles of a tar-
get user and similar users.
Jang et al. (2023)
presented a method that enables a chatbot to
adapt its responses over time by training it on
a dataset encoding elapsed time and multiple
types of interpersonal relationships.
Xu et al.
(2022); Zhong et al. (2024); Packer et al. (2023);
Bae et al. (2022); Lee et al. (2023); Lim et al.
(2022) introduced approaches that extract per-
sonal data from user utterances, store it, and gen-
erate responses based on that information. While
these methods personalize chatbot responses,
they do not address the proactive initiation of con-
versations, which is a key aspect of our research.

Architecture

target users as topic candidates, allowing them to
be reused to enrich future conversations.

2.4. Conversational Recommender
Systems
Conversational recommender systems (CRS)
are designed to actively elicit user prefer-
ences through conversation and recommend
items based on those insights (Friedman et al.,
2023; Deldjoo et al., 2024). Several studies
have focused on improving user engagement
and recommendation success. For instance,
Hayati et al. (2020) integrated sociable recom-
mendation strategies into CRS, while Wang et al.
(2022) combined recommendation and conver-
sation modules. Other studies have evaluated
whether LLMs can accurately recommend items
in zero-shot settings. Kang et al. (2023); Liu et al.
(2023); Sanner et al. (2023); Sileo et al. (2022);
He et al. (2023) constructed prompts that merge
user preferences with instructions to recommend
or evaluate items. Although these studies share
our goal of understanding user preferences for
proactive recommendations, they do not estimate
user knowledge or assess the user’s familiarity
with the recommended items.
3. Proposed Method: Topic-Initiator
3.1. Architecture
As introduced in Section 1, Topic-Initiator follows
an iterative process to continuously provide new
topics that align with a target user’s interests. The
overall procedure consists of three mains steps (A
to C), illustrated in Figure 2.
A. Information Gathering: After interacting with
a user, Topic-Initiator proactively gathers relevant
information based on the conversation content.
Speciﬁcally, it employs an LLM to generate search
queries from the conversation and conducts web
searches to collect topic candidates. Additionally,
Topic-Initiator stores past conversations with non-
target users as topic candidates, allowing them to
be reused to enrich future conversations.
B. PT-RAG: Topic-Initiator uses PT-RAG to re-
trieve a new and interesting topic for the user. The
main components of PT-RAG are as follows (ex-
plained in detail in the next section):

3.2.
Personalized-Topic RAG (PT-RAG)
PT-RAG is designed to retrieve a new and inter-
esting topic for a user by leveraging LLM inference
to identify a topic candidate that are absent from
a user’s inferred knowledge (derived from previ-
ously disclosed information). Because supplying
a full dump of a user’s knowledge or the entire
candidate pool is impractical given input-length
and scale constraints, PT-RAG groups both user
knowledge and candidates into topic categories
(e.g., music, travel) and performs category-guided
retrieval, providing the LLM only with category-
relevant summaries and candidates.

4.2.4. Results
The results are presented in Figure 6. The hor-
izontal axis in Figure 6 represents the n-th con-
versation, while the vertical axis shows the win-
ning rate in the A/B tests. As shown in Fig-
ures 6(a) and 6(b), a signiﬁcantly larger num-
ber of participants preferred conversing with either
the Topic-Initiator chatbot or the proactive chat-
bot compared to the baseline. Furthermore, Fig-
ure 6(c) indicates that during the ﬁrst conversa-
tion, signiﬁcantly more participants preferred the
proactive chatbot over Topic-Initiator. However,
as the interactions progressed, more participants
favored Topic-Initiator over the proactive chatbot,
with a signiﬁcant preference emerging from the
third conversation onward. These results highlight
that the importance of taking initiative in conver-
sation to stimulate user’s willingness to converse.
Additionally, they emphasize the role of topic se-
lection. When the proactive chatbot asked about
information previously disclosed by the user, it in-
creased the user’s willingness to converse. This
is likely because it demonstrated that the chat-
bot remembered past interactions. This ﬁnding is
consistent with Tsunomori et al. (2021). However,
maintaining user’s willingness solely through such
methods proved difﬁcult, as indicated by the re-
sults. In contrast, providing users with fresh and
interesting topics helped sustain and further en-
hance their willingness to continue conversations.
We provide an example of a conversation from the
human evaluation that aligns with this analysis in
Appendix B.
5. Conclusion
We proposed Topic-Initiator, a chatbot that con-
tinuously and proactively provides users with new
and interesting topics. To obtain such topics, it
collects both web-crawled data and conversations
with other users. To enable Topic-Initiator to re-
trieve new and interesting topics for users, we
also introduced a novel RAG framework called PT-
RAG. PT-RAG estimates user interests and knowl-
edge, organizes both user data and collected data
into topic categories, identiﬁes relevant categories
based on user interests, and retrieves new topics
within those categories based on user knowledge
by leveraging the inference capabilities of LLMs.
Our ﬁndings addressed the research questions as
follows: RQ1: Through automatic evaluations, we
demonstrated that PT-RAG more accurately ob-
tains new and interesting topics for users com-
pared with existing RAG methods. RQ2: Through
human evaluation of the Topic-Initiator chatbot, we
showed that users were more willing to converse
with our system than with chatbots that either talk
known topics or remained passive.
Topic-Initiator focuses on stimulating the willing-
ness during subsequent conversation initiations.
In our future works, we intend to extend our
method to enhance the willingness during other
phases of interaction.
Limitations
Starting the ﬁrst conversation: As described in
Section 4.2.1, Topic-Initiator currently faces chal-
lenges in initiating ﬁrst conversations with users
because it lacks prior knowledge about users it
has not previously interacted with. To overcome
this limitation, it is crucial to identify which spe-
ciﬁc chatbots abilities are most effective in stim-
